The complete Python programs use NumPy arrays with rows as observations and columns as features; the mathematical deeper branches are optional on a first pass.} sections={headings.map(heading => [headingId(heading), heading.replace(/^\d+\. /, '')])}> Learn to build groups when you have measurements but no supplied group labels. You will move representatives through a point cloud, construct and cut a merge tree, fit a real geyser dataset, turn pixel colors into a palette, and decide what evidence supports a useful result. Every lab asks for a prediction before you touch a control; the exercises change the numbers so you cannot copy the demonstration. Your first pass: read sections 1 through 9, running the five labs and the first three programs as you meet them, then finish with the practice in 13. Sections 10 and 14 are complete applications you can return to; 11 and 12 are deeper branches about scale and alternative objectives. You should finish able to trace an assignment and mean update by hand, read a dendrogram height under its convention, explain why a real dataset splits where it does, and say what a low error does and does not tell you.

{headings[0]}

Old Faithful, the geyser in Yellowstone, was watched for two weeks in August 1985. For 272 eruptions someone recorded how long the eruption lasted and how long the next visitor had to wait for another. The park’s practical question was simple: after watching an eruption, how long should we tell people to wait? Nobody labeled the eruptions as “short type” or “long type.” The data are just two numbers per row. Two dense regions are visible, but a picture is not a decision. Clustering turns a chosen notion of similarity into groups. Before choosing an algorithm, fix three things: what one observation is, which measurements describe it, and what decision the groups will support. Here an observation is one eruption, the measurements are two durations in minutes, and the decision is a waiting-time recommendation. Change any of the three and you have a different clustering problem on the same file. A clustering algorithm always returns groups. It optimizes a numerical objective on the geometry you gave it, and it will find a partition of pure noise just as readily as a partition of two real regimes. Everything that follows separates two questions: did the optimizer do its job, and are the resulting groups useful for the decision? A good fit answers the first. Only evidence from outside the objective answers the second. We say this once here so we do not have to say it after every result. The k in k-means counts representatives. In KNN it counted neighbors consulted for a prediction. K-means never looks at supplied class labels; it learns centers from the feature vectors alone. You still choose k. A hierarchy postpones the choice of a flat group count, but it does not remove the choices of distance, linkage and resolution. To calculate by hand we need something smaller than 272 rows. We will carry six constructed points through the center and merge investigations, then return to the geyser once the mechanisms are clear. P0 through P5 are observation IDs; a cluster label is a separate number. We will ask two things of these points: which two centers represent them well, and what sequence of groups appears if we merge the closest pair again and again. Two inspection teams call for two representatives; exploring several resolutions calls for a hierarchy.

{headings[1]}

Start with two tentative centers at P0=(1,0) and P4=(7,5). For each point, calculate its squared distance to each center and choose the smaller. Squaring avoids a square root without changing which distance is smallest. P2=(3,2) has squared distances (3−1)²+(2−0)²=8 and (3−7)²+(2−5)²=25, so it chooses the first center. After every point has chosen, move each center to the coordinate-wise mean of its assigned points. The first four points choose the first center, whose new position is ((1+1.5+3+3.5)/4, (0+.5+2+2)/4)=(2.25, 1.125). The other two produce (7.25, 5.25). Now repeat: new centers may change which center is closest. This alternation is Lloyd’s algorithm. The quantity being reduced is the sum of squared distances from each observation to its assigned center: squared error, within-cluster sum of squares or inertia. The initial assignment costs 19.25. Moving to the two means reduces it to 7.6875. Keep this number in mind; it returns in section 7 by a completely different route. Two things to notice in the lab. First, the pale boundary line is the set of points equally far from both centers. Assignment simply asks which side of that line a point is on, so labels can only change when a center moves and drags the line across a point. Second, a fixed point is reached when an assignment leaves every label unchanged; the objective then has nowhere to go. That is the algorithm finishing its job, and it is a different statement from “these are the right groups.” The mean is a representative vector, not necessarily an observed item. For values 1, 2, 9 the mean is 4 even though nobody supplied a 4. If the task requires selecting an existing photograph, document or machine as an exemplar, that constraint calls for a different representative, such as a medoid. Section 12 returns to that choice. It is equally distant from both. Specify a deterministic tie rule, such as choosing the lower-index center. Odd k does not prevent a nearest-center tie; that idea concerns binary voting ties in KNN. The label chosen at the boundary does not change this point’s squared error.

{headings[2]}

Distance adds differences across columns, so units matter before any center is learned. Suppose two customers differ by 1,000 dollars and 1 visit. Raw squared distance is 1,000,001. Writing the same money difference in thousands of dollars makes it 1²+1²=2. No customer changed; the numerical meaning of “near” did. The geyser shows the same effect on real data. Waiting times range over about 50 minutes and eruption durations over about 3.5 minutes. In raw units the waiting column dominates every distance, so k-means with two centers splits almost entirely on waiting time. After standardizing both columns the split uses both measurements. The two partitions agree on most eruptions but not all: 4 of the 272 rows change side, and both centers move. The library program in section 8 prints both fits. Choose a meaningful scale for each feature, then express a difference relative to that scale. If a difference of 1,000 dollars should matter as much as one visit, divide dollars by 1,000 before using Euclidean distance. Alternatively, state weights explicitly. A nonnegative weight w_r multiplies the squared difference in column r. To implement that weight by transforming coordinates, multiply the column by √w_r, not by w_r. {'\\begin{gathered}d_w(x,y)^2=\\sum_{r=1}^{d}w_r(x_r-y_r)^2,\\\\ z_r=\\sqrt{w_r}\\,x_r.\\end{gathered}'} Converting every coordinate from meters to centimeters multiplies all squared distances by 10,000 and leaves nearest-center choices unchanged, provided the centers are converted too. Changing one column’s scale changes that column’s relative importance. To preserve an existing distance when x_r becomes a·x_r, divide its squared-distance weight by a². Standardization subtracts a training mean and divides by a training standard deviation, making a one-standard-deviation difference equally costly in every column. It is a sensible default and a modeling choice: a nearly constant noisy column or a rare binary flag can gain large influence. Centering alone does not change pairwise Euclidean distances; scaling does. A constant feature carries no distance information and needs safe handling rather than division by zero. Missing values are not zeros. Nominal category IDs such as red=1, blue=2, green=3 do not supply meaningful Euclidean intervals. Counts may benefit from a justified transform when relative differences matter. Write these choices down before looking for attractive clusters.

Run the examples in your own environment

The visual labs run on this page. The Python blocks are complete programs with recorded outputs; they do not execute in the browser. In a terminal with Python 3.12 available, create a project folder, change into it and run python -m venv .venv. Use py -3.12 on Windows or python3.12 on macOS/Linux instead of python if that is your installation’s command. Activate the environment with .venv\Scripts\activate.bat in Windows Command Prompt, or source .venv/bin/activate in a macOS/Linux shell. Then install the versions used for the recorded results: {'python -m pip install numpy==2.3.5 scipy==1.18.1 scikit-learn==1.9.1'} Save the next complete Python block as clustering_scaling.py in that folder and run python clustering_scaling.py. Save each later block in its own descriptively named file; each contains its own imports and inputs. If activation is unavailable, invoke the environment’s Python directly: .venv\Scripts\python.exe on Windows or .venv/bin/python on macOS/Linux. Compare the printed result with the recorded output before changing a fixture. Read the two comparisons separately: a pure change of units with compensating weights preserves a distance; a change of feature importance can change the partition. The held-out transformation uses scales learned on training rows only, so the distant final device still receives a label. A label is an assignment, not a certificate that the device resembles its group.

{headings[3]}

Write the two unknowns separately

Let X contain n row vectors x_i in d dimensions. Let μ_j be center j and a_i the index assigned to row i. We choose k centers and assignments to make the following sum small. The norm squared means “sum of squared coordinate differences,” and J is the total error. {'\\begin{gathered}J(a,\\mu)=\\sum_{i=1}^{n}\\|x_i-\\mu_{a_i}\\|^2,\\\\ a_i\\in\\{1,\\ldots,k\\}.\\end{gathered}'} For fixed centers, each row contributes its own term, and choosing the nearest center minimizes that term independently. For fixed assignments, each center influences only its own group, and the mean minimizes that group’s squared error. These two easy subproblems are why alternating updates are practical even though the joint problem is hard: minimizing J exactly over all partitions is NP-hard, even for k=2 in general dimension and even for points in the plane. Lloyd’s algorithm is a heuristic for a problem nobody can solve exactly at scale, which is why initialization matters so much. {'\\begin{gathered}a_i\\leftarrow\\operatorname*{argmin}_{j}\\|x_i-\\mu_j\\|^2,\\\\ \\mu_j\\leftarrow\\frac{1}{|C_j|}\\sum_{i\\in C_j}x_i\\quad (|C_j|>0).\\end{gathered}'} C_j is the set of observation indices currently assigned to center j. The mean requires a nonempty group. Ties and empty groups need explicit rules in code. For a group C with mean m, write x−c=(x−m)+(m−c) and expand the square. Summing eliminates the cross term because Σ(x−m)=0. The remaining identity gives both the minimizer and exactly how much a misplaced center costs. {'\\begin{aligned}\\sum_{x\\in C}\\|x-c\\|^2&=\\sum_{x\\in C}\\|x-m\\|^2\\\\ &\\quad+|C|\\|m-c\\|^2.\\end{aligned}'} The second term is nonnegative and is zero exactly at c=m. No calculus is needed, though differentiating gives the same answer: the gradient in c is 2|C|c−2Σx. With nonnegative observation weights v_i and positive total group weight, replace the mean by Σv_ix_i/Σv_i and the objective by Σv_i‖x_i−μ_a_i‖². A weight of three has the same objective contribution as three identical copies of a row. Observation weights and feature weights solve different problems. For fixed nonnegative feature weights shared by all centers, the coordinate-wise weighted metric still has the ordinary observation mean as an optimum in each positively weighted coordinate. A zero-weight coordinate does not affect the objective and should not be read as a learned discriminating feature.

Initialization changes the route through the objective

A good first center does not make the second one obvious. Randomly chosen rows can fall in the same region. K-means++ spreads the starting opportunities by giving each row a probability proportional to its current squared distance D_i² to its nearest selected center. First choose one row uniformly, then repeatedly sample from these probabilities and update the nearest-center distances. {'\\begin{gathered}P(\\text{next center}=x_i)=\\frac{D_i^2}{\\sum_r D_r^2},\\\\ D_i^2=\\min_{c\\in\\text{selected}}\\|x_i-c\\|^2.\\end{gathered}'} For one-dimensional rows 0, 2, 5 with 0 already selected, squared distances are 0, 4, 25. The next probabilities are 0, 4/29, 25/29. The farthest point is likely, but point 2 still has a chance. Choosing the farthest every time is a different rule, and the lab below shows how different: on our six points the farthest row wins less than half of the draws. When every row already coincides with a selected center, all D_i² are zero and there is no distribution to sample from. Extra centers cannot reduce an error that is already zero. The lab exposes this stopping condition; the runnable implementation shows how to honor a requested k anyway by choosing an unused row, which can create a duplicate center and leave fewer than k occupied groups. For the original unweighted Euclidean D²-sampling algorithm, Arthur and Vassilvitskii prove E[J_seed]≤8(ln k+2)J*, where J* is the globally optimal k-center squared error and the expectation is over the random initialization. Non-increasing Lloyd updates cannot worsen that bound. It is a guarantee about expected objective value, not a promise that every run places one center in each visually intended group. The theorem is for vanilla D² sampling. Current scikit-learn KMeans uses a greedy k-means++ variant that considers several candidate centers per selection and keeps the best. Sharing the name does not transfer the theorem. Multiple initializations compare candidate fits by the same objective; they improve the odds without certifying the global optimum.

{headings[4]}

Every exact assignment and mean-update half-step is non-increasing in J. It may leave J unchanged because the best choice was already in place or a point is tied. Being bounded below by zero is not by itself a proof that an iterative algorithm stops: the positive sequence 1, 1/2, 1/4, … never reaches zero in finitely many terms. The finite-data argument needs one more ingredient. With a deterministic tie rule and retained empty centers, the assignment is a function of the centers, and the centers are a function of the assignment. Whenever a nonempty mean actually changes, the identity above gives a strict decrease in J. There are finitely many assignments, so finitely many possible center configurations, so the strict decreases must stop, and once the centers stop moving the labels stop too. Floating-point implementations add an iteration limit and usually a tolerance. How many iterations? In practice usually a few dozen. In the worst case, Vattani constructed planar point sets on which Lloyd’s algorithm needs 2^Ω(n) iterations. The gap between theory and practice is explained by smoothed analysis: Arthur, Manthey and Röglin showed that after tiny random perturbation of the input, the expected number of iterations is polynomial. Real measurements come with their own noise, which is why the pathological cases are not seen in the wild. A stopped loop is not necessarily a fixed point. If an iteration limit interrupts the updates, reassigning points to the returned centers may change labels, and those centers may no longer equal the means of their returned groups. Report that status instead of printing “converged” because the loop ended. At an ordinary fixed point both conditional choices are optimal; ties and empty centers complicate stronger local-optimum statements, and there is no global-optimum guarantee. The rectangle in the center investigation makes the distinction concrete. Four points (0,0), (0,1), (3,0), (3,1) with k=2 can stabilize as a bottom and top group with centers (1.5,0) and (1.5,1) and total squared error 9. Left and right groups have centers (0,.5) and (3,.5) and error 1. Both are fixed points under their own centers. Stability alone does not identify the better one. The algorithm is about thirty lines: a distance matrix, an argmin, a per-cluster mean, and a check that reassignment changes nothing. Validation is a single finiteness check so the mechanism stays visible; a library adds far more. The returned inertia is recalculated from the returned labels and centers. Look at the deliberately short run and the duplicate fixture as carefully as the favorable blob example: matching a library’s error on one dataset is useful verification, not proof of optimality. The scratch program is for learning and small controlled checks. Production fitting needs optimized distance kernels, careful numerical behavior, stopping diagnostics and input validation. Do not replace a mature implementation with this one because the sample output agrees.

{headings[5]}

Instead of moving centers and allowing memberships to change, begin with six singleton groups and repeatedly join two groups. After the first merge there are five groups; after five merges there is one. The whole merge history is a dendrogram, a tree whose leaves are observations and whose internal nodes are merges. Agglomerative means building upward by joining; divisive methods build downward by splitting. To choose the next merge, define how far apart two existing groups are. Four common linkage rules use the same input points but summarize their cross-group relationships differently. Ordinary Euclidean distance has the coordinate unit; squared error has its square. For our six points, Ward first joins P2 and P3. They are 0.5 apart; their new mean is (3.25, 2). P0/P1 and P4/P5 then form two more pairs. On this fixture all four linkages happen to produce the same tree shape, differing only in heights, because the three pairs are so much tighter than anything between them. That is why the lab offers a second configuration: a chain of six evenly spaced points plus a compact triple. There single linkage swallows the whole chain one link at a time, while complete linkage refuses to extend it and splits it in half. The table’s warnings become visible behavior. The tree’s leaf labels read “observation · cluster”: P4·2 means observation P4 currently belongs to group 2. Group numbers only distinguish the current groups; they are neither quantities nor a ranking. Read the axes before the colors. In the scatter view, horizontal and vertical position are feature coordinates. In the dendrogram, vertical height is the merge score under its stated convention, and horizontal leaf placement is chosen only to draw the tree legibly. Rotating the two children of any branch changes the left-to-right order while preserving the hierarchy. Adjacent leaves are not necessarily each other’s nearest observations. A horizontal threshold includes merges at or below that height. Branches connected below the line form a cluster. Alternatively, apply exactly a chosen number of recorded merges to obtain a chosen count. With equal merge heights these are different policies: a threshold includes all tied merges together, while a merge-count prefix can stop partway through the tied operations. Our Ward tree has two successive merges at √.5≈.707107. Just below that height there are five groups; at that height both tied pairs are joined, leaving three. No horizontal threshold produces exactly four groups on this tree. A four-group merge prefix depends on the declared order of the tied merges, so reporting the cut convention is part of reporting the result. A tree with dozens of leaves is read differently from a tree with six. Individual leaf labels stop mattering; what you look for is a tall empty stretch between consecutive merge heights, because every cut inside that stretch gives the same partition. On the geyser subsample the final merge is about five times higher than the one before it, which is strong evidence that two groups is the resolution this geometry supports. Lower in the tree the gaps are small and the partition changes with every nudge of the cut. No. All ancestor relationships and merge heights remain the same. Only the drawing’s leaf order changes. A dendrogram is a record of the selected algorithm’s merges; it is not automatically a family tree, an evolutionary model or a causal explanation.

{headings[6]}

Ward asks a particularly useful question: how much extra squared error must we pay if A and B are represented by one mean instead of two? Let their sizes be a and b and their means m_A and m_B. The combined mean is (a m_A+b m_B)/(a+b). Moving A’s representative to that mean adds a‖m_A−m_AB‖²; moving B’s adds b‖m_B−m_AB‖². The scatter already inside each group appears on both sides of the comparison and cancels. {'\\begin{aligned}\\Delta&=\\operatorname{SSE}(A\\cup B)\\\\ &\\quad-\\operatorname{SSE}(A)-\\operatorname{SSE}(B),\\\\ &=\\frac{ab}{a+b}\\|m_A-m_B\\|^2.\\end{aligned}'} Two groups with the same center separation can have different Ward costs. Merging two singletons separated by 2 costs (1/2)·4=2. Merging two groups of 100 with that separation costs (10,000/200)·4=200. Ward penalizes giving many observations a worse representative; it is not nearest-centroid linkage. SciPy’s Euclidean Ward linkage height is h=√(2Δ). Thus h²=2Δ and Δ=h²/2. The height has distance units; Δ has squared-distance units. For two singletons, h equals their Euclidean distance. For larger groups it generally does not equal the distance between their means. This is not a SciPy quirk: Murtagh and Legendre showed in 2014 that two different algorithms circulate under Ward’s name in statistical software, one working on distances and one on squared distances, and that they produce different trees from the same input. Always check which one you are reading. Once the three pairs have formed, their internal squared errors sum to .125+.25+.25=.625. Merging the first two pairs adds 7.0625, giving 7.6875 for the two-group partition. Adding the final cost gives 63.708333… for the single group. Summing all Ward increments recovers the total one-group scatter, a telescoping identity that gives an independent check on any merge implementation. The two-group Ward cut costs 7.6875. Lloyd’s algorithm in section 2 stopped at 7.6875. That is not a coincidence: both methods minimize the same within-group squared error, and on these six points both arrive at the same partition {'{P0,P1,P2,P3}'} versus {'{P4,P5}'}. They travel differently. Lloyd can move any point at any time but depends on where it started; Ward never revisits a merge but never depends on a random start. When the two disagree on a dataset, the disagreement itself is informative: either Lloyd is stuck in a local optimum or an early greedy merge committed Ward to a partition the mean-based route can improve. A common practical trick uses a Ward cut to initialize k-means, combining Ward’s determinism with Lloyd’s ability to repair a point-level mistake. Because m_A−m_AB=b(m_A−m_B)/(a+b) and m_B−m_AB=−a(m_A−m_B)/(a+b), the two movement penalties sum to [ab²+ba²]/(a+b)² times ‖m_A−m_B‖². Cancelling gives ab/(a+b). The same parallel-axis identity proved the k-means mean update: the methods share an error measure while taking different routes through possible partitions. Greedily minimizing the next Ward increment does not minimize the total error for every eventual k. Earlier merges cannot be undone. Nor does Ward guarantee spherical or equal-cardinality groups; its score favors compact solutions in the chosen Euclidean geometry without enforcing those conditions. Single linkage has a different useful connection: at a distance threshold t, make a graph connecting observations whose distance is at most t. Its connected components are the single-linkage clusters at t. A minimum spanning tree preserves those threshold connections, so cutting its edges above t yields the same groups. This explains both efficient single-linkage constructions and the chaining effect: connectivity through a path does not require close endpoints. All four linkages taught here produce monotone trees: each merge is at least as high as the merges below it. Centroid and median linkage do not have this property. Merging two groups can move their new centroid closer to a third group than either was before, producing an inversion where a parent sits below its child and the height axis stops being readable as a threshold. The MIT lecture linked below uses centroid linkage in its example, so keep that caveat in mind when watching it. The scratch merge implementation computes each candidate cost from actual group sizes and means and compares the result to SciPy. The output distinguishes a linkage row’s children, height and merged observation count. Compare pair membership rather than raw label numbers, and inspect the at-most-k behavior of fcluster(..., criterion='maxclust') at tied heights. A SciPy linkage input can be an n×d observation matrix or a one-dimensional condensed distance vector containing n(n−1)/2 distinct pair distances. A square n×n distance matrix is not silently equivalent: passed as observations, its rows would themselves become feature vectors. Use the documented conversion for precomputed distances. Ward must receive Euclidean geometry; already-squared distances are also not the correct input for its usual height convention.

{headings[7]}

Before running a library example, identify its input, learned state and prediction rule. KMeans fits centers and exposes training labels_ and inertia_. predict assigns new transformed rows to centers. Cluster 0 is not “low,” cluster 1 is not “high,” and a large distance does not produce a rejected or noise label. The native examples below were executed with Python 3.12.14, NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.18.1 and scikit-learn 1.9.1. Set random_state, initialization and n_init explicitly, and record versions rather than expecting identical defaults forever. Small floating-point differences and tied label numbering can still vary across environments. The geyser data are embedded in the program so it runs offline. Read the standardized and raw-unit fits side by side: the same algorithm, the same k, and centers that differ because the geometry differs. Then read the k sweep with section 9 in mind. The blob comparison at the end is retained from the earlier lesson: three estimators agree perfectly on generated data, which tells you the data are easy, not that the estimators are interchangeable. In the checked KMeans API, n_init='auto' uses one initialization for k-means++ and ten for random or callable initialization. Explicit repeated starts make the experimental choice clear. KMeans chooses its best fit among runs. MiniBatchKMeans uses its initialization count to choose a starting configuration before one mini-batch optimization run, which is a different contract. Read the parameter documentation rather than transferring the interpretation by name. Library stopping may use small center movement rather than exact assignment stabilization. The KMeans documentation explains that early stopping can leave centers inconsistent with the means of the final labels; it reassigns labels to agree with prediction on the returned centers. That is why the scratch example distinguishes a complete fixed point from a coherent but early-stopped return. AgglomerativeClustering provides a flat partition for a selected cluster count or a distance threshold. For a complete inspectable tree, SciPy’s linkage matrix is convenient. Ward requires Euclidean distance. Single, complete and average can use other dissimilarities, but their results then answer those different distance questions. {headings[8]}

More representatives can describe more detail. At the global optimum, allowing another center cannot increase the minimum squared error: the old solution can be kept while the extra center does no work, or a group can be split. With one center per distinct observation the error is zero. Minimizing training inertia across k therefore selects the largest k you try, unless something else is paying for complexity. An elbow plot looks for a change in the rate of improvement. On a linear axis the geyser curve is a cliff followed by a floor, which hides everything after k=2. The logarithmic axis above turns equal proportional improvements into equal vertical drops, and the story becomes readable: one center to two removes most of the error, two to three removes a further third, and each later center buys less. Separately fitted local solutions can even show a small increase as k grows because the optimizer found a worse candidate; retry before treating that as a property of the objective. The silhouette compares a point’s average distance to other members of its own group, a(i), with the smallest average distance to another group, b(i). For a nonsingleton group and a positive denominator, s(i)=(b(i)−a(i))/max(a(i),b(i)). A score near 1 means within-group neighbors are closer under this distance; near 0 means the averages are similar; a negative score means another group has the smaller average distance. {'\\begin{gathered}s(i)=\\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\\max(a(i),b(i))},\\\\ -1\\le s(i)\\le1.\\end{gathered}'} For a hand calculation, put 0 and 1 in group A and 4 and 6 in group B. For the point 1, its within-group mean distance is a=|1−0|=1. Its average distance to B is b=(|1−4|+|1−6|)/2=4. Its silhouette is (4−1)/4=.75. Notice that b averages over the other group, not just its closest point or its center. The usual implementation convention gives a singleton silhouette of zero, and scikit-learn’s overall score requires between 2 and n−1 distinct labels, which is why the figure shows k=1 as undefined. A mean silhouette can hide one poor group, so inspect group sizes and individual values. On the geyser the median silhouette peaks sharply at k=2 and the five random starts agree exactly there, while from k=3 on they disagree. Both signals point the same way as the dendrogram gap, and all three come from the same geometry, so they are three views of one fact rather than three independent confirmations. Relabeling [0,0,1,1] as [7,7,3,3] leaves the partition unchanged. Comparing raw labels row by row would call every row different. Compare which pairs share a group, or use a permutation-invariant measure. The adjusted Rand index (ARI) accounts for chance agreement under its reference model; it is not an accuracy and may be negative. The later Clustering Evaluation & Validation lesson develops these metrics and their assumptions. A sensible workflow chooses a small plausible range of k, compares repeated fits and profiles, checks sensitivity to justified representations, then freezes a decision before its evaluation. For future-row quantization, hold out rows and report average nearest-center squared error with the same training-owned transform. For an exploratory description of one fixed collection, fitting all rows can be appropriate; say so, rather than implying a generalization test was performed. For the geyser, the useful downstream check is the original question: does telling visitors “about 55 minutes after a short eruption, about 80 after a long one” beat a single average wait? It does. The typical error of a single average wait is about 14 minutes; within the two fitted groups it is about 6 minutes, a reduction of roughly 80% in waiting-time variance. That is a claim about usefulness, and the objective alone could never make it. The gap statistic compares observed within-cluster dispersion with dispersion from simulated reference datasets intended to have no cluster structure. One common form subtracts observed log dispersion from its expected log value under the reference. Its recommendation depends on the null generator, Monte Carlo variability and selection rule. A uniform reference in a bounding box is a modeling choice, not a universal definition of “no clusters.” For resampling stability, compare partitions on a common set of observations. A KMeans fit from each resample can predict a fixed probe set. A hierarchy needs an explicitly chosen comparison on shared sampled observations or another justified out-of-sample rule. Comparing unrelated bootstrap row positions compares different objects, even if both label vectors have the same length.

{headings[9]}

An image provides a concrete use for representatives. Treat each pixel’s three color channels as a vector x_i=(R,G,B). Fit k centers, then replace each pixel by its assigned center’s color. The result is vector quantization: representing many possible vectors with a finite codebook. Here “cluster label” becomes a palette index, and squared error becomes a measurable reconstruction cost. The three images are constructed in code so that their data, pixel counts and calculations are inspectable. Increasing k preserves more color detail but does not recover spatial boundaries: the clustering sees colors, not pixel coordinates. Two distant pixels with identical RGB values contribute identically. That is exactly right for a global color palette and insufficient for segmenting connected objects. Repeated colors offer an exact reduction. If a color occurs 40 times, store it once with observation weight 40. Weighted squared error over unique colors equals squared error over every original pixel for the same centers. Unweighted unique-color clustering would make a once-occurring accent as influential as a dominant background; the sky image shows the sun losing its color first for exactly this reason, while the gradient image, where every count is one, shows what quantization does when weighting cannot help. Separate the floating-point centers from the byte-valued palette actually stored. Rounding channels changes both the reconstruction error and, after reassignment, the nearest palette choice. The output checks the equivalent weighted and repeated objectives and scores the stored reconstruction rather than a palette that was never written. For N pixels in a raw 8-bit RGB representation, the color payload is 24N bits. A toy indexed representation with k≤256 byte RGB palette entries takes 24k palette bits plus N⌈log₂k⌉ index bits, ignoring dimensions, headers, padding and coding details. This is bookkeeping for a specified format, not a prediction of PNG or JPEG file sizes, which also exploit spatial structure. Squared distance in encoded sRGB channel values is a teaching objective, not a model of perceived color difference. A perceptually motivated color space changes the problem and has its own conversion details. Choose the metric for the visual task. This connection explains a historical name. Stuart Lloyd worked out the alternating assignment-and-mean procedure in 1957 as a Bell Labs technical note on least-squares quantization for pulse-code modulation, the digitization of telephone signals. It circulated privately for a quarter of a century and was finally published in 1982, by which time the same idea had been rediscovered several times under other names. Representatives need not be categories with human names; they can be codebook values that trade storage against distortion. The same center-assignment mechanism can also organize a search index, as the next section shows.

{headings[10]}

A direct dense Lloyd assignment compares n rows with k centers across d coordinates, costing O(nkd) work per iteration; mean accumulation adds O(nd). With I iterations and r complete starts, the main bound is O(rInkd), excluding initialization and input processing. Chunking distance calculations avoids materializing every row-center-coordinate difference at once. Keeping the dense input costs O(nd) storage, centers O(kd) and labels O(n). A broadcasted NumPy demonstration may additionally materialize O(nkd) differences, while a chunked production implementation avoids that temporary. Elkan-style acceleration uses triangle-inequality bounds to skip some distance computations at the cost of extra O(nk) memory; it changes the speed, not the objective.

Update representatives from small batches

Mini-batch k-means updates from a small subset rather than recomputing every full-data mean each step. The incremental-mean identity explains its basic update: if a center represents t assigned observations with mean m and a new assigned point is x, the combined mean is (tm+x)/(t+1)=m+(x−m)/(t+1). The new point’s influence shrinks as the count grows. {'m_{t+1}=m_t+\\frac{x-m_t}{t+1}.'} This running summary reflects assignments made while centers were changing; it is not the mean of a freshly reassigned full dataset, and individual mini-batch steps need not decrease full-data inertia. A count-based learning rate also adapts slowly to genuine drift; forgetting old data is a separate modeling decision.

A merge tree can be expensive before it is drawn

There are n(n−1)/2 distinct pair distances. For n=10,000, storing just those values as float64 needs 399,960,000 bytes, about 381.4 MiB, before data and algorithm overhead. At n=100,000 it is about 40 billion bytes. A small dendrogram view does not reduce the computation needed to build a full dense hierarchy. The scratch Ward implementation repeatedly considers active pairs for clarity. SciPy’s documented implementations for single, complete, average and Ward use O(n²) time for the clustering stage and O(n²) memory, with method-specific algorithms; computing dense high-dimensional input distances adds its own work. A sparse connectivity constraint reduces candidate merges but changes which merges are admissible, so it changes the problem as well as the resource use. BIRCH builds a compact tree of subcluster summaries. For a subcluster, store its count N, vector sum LS and sum of squared norms SS. Its mean is LS/N and its within-group squared error is SS−‖LS‖²/N. This follows by expanding every ‖x−mean‖²; the summary can be updated without retaining every row. If a later center c must represent that whole subcluster, its cost is the subcluster’s internal error plus N‖mean−c‖². Weighted clustering of subcluster means therefore reproduces the objective for that restricted assignment problem, up to a constant. It cannot recover a better original partition that would split a compressed subcluster. The checked scikit-learn BIRCH global-clustering path does not pass subcluster counts as sample weights, so do not attribute this exact weighted objective to that API without implementing it. The identity has a numerical caveat: SS−‖LS‖²/N subtracts similar large quantities when data have a large offset and tiny variance. Stable centered or incremental calculations matter in floating point.

Use a codebook to route a nearest-neighbor search

In an inverted-file vector index, first learn coarse centers. Assign each database vector to a center and store its ID in that center’s list. At query time, find a few close centers and search their lists. For a toy database split across four lists, probing one list avoids examining the other three. It can also miss the true nearest vector near a list boundary. The cluster assignment is now a routing decision. More lists or fewer probed lists change work and recall together. Faiss’s IVF indexes implement this family of ideas. Measure recall against exact search on representative held-out queries and record index size and latency under actual conditions; a low training inertia says nothing about retrieval quality.

Every point assigned to one of two distinct Euclidean centers is separated from the other center’s points by a straight equal-distance boundary, the line you watched in the first lab. With more centers, each nearest-center region is an intersection of half-spaces: a convex Voronoi cell. That geometry suits compact regions and cannot represent every intended shape. A large, spread-out group may receive several centers while a small nearby group shares one. Unequal density, imbalance and outliers change squared-error contributions; none is diagnosed by k alone. Because the loss is squared, moving an outlier from distance 10 to distance 100 multiplies its contribution from 100 to 10,000, and k-means will still assign it to a center. A separate distance threshold needs its own data and validation before it becomes an anomaly detector. For unit vectors x and y, ‖x−y‖²=2−2xᵀy. Nearest unit centers therefore maximize cosine similarity. But the mean of normalized rows need not have unit length. Ordinary k-means retains that mean, whereas spherical k-means renormalizes a nonzero group sum and uses a directional assignment objective. Zero vectors or cancelling group sums need explicit treatment. Normalizing the input alone does not make those procedures equivalent. Kernel k-means uses the same mean-squared-error idea after an implicit mapping φ. For a group C, distance to its feature-space mean expands to K(x,x)−(2/|C|)Σ_y∈C K(x,y)+(1/|C|²)Σ_y,z∈C K(y,z). A valid positive-semidefinite kernel makes this an inner-product geometry. The formula can model curved input-space boundaries without constructing φ, but pairwise kernel storage and the kernel choice introduce real costs and assumptions. As σ² approaches zero, a uniquely nearest component receives limiting responsibility one, and the weighted mean update approaches the hard-assignment mean. Exact ties do not automatically choose one component; finite-variance EM remains soft, and unequal priors shift its comparisons. // Complete standalone programs, executed by the semantic native verifier.
export const clusteringExamples = {
  "lloyd": {
    "title": "Implement vanilla D² seeding and Lloyd’s algorithm from scratch",
    "question": "If the last mean update changes the nearest-center assignments, has the algorithm reached a fixed point? What should it return when its iteration budget ends there?",
    "code": "import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs


def check_points(values):
    # Accept a finite numeric row-by-feature matrix and nothing else.
    points = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    if points.ndim != 2 or not np.isfinite(points).all():
        raise ValueError("Use a finite numeric row-by-feature matrix.")
    return points


def squared_distances(points, centers):
    # Return the n × k matrix of squared Euclidean distances.
    return ((points[:, None, :] - centers[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=2)


def d2_seed(points, k, seed=0):
    # Vanilla k-means++: a uniform first row, then D²-proportional draws.
    points = check_points(points)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    chosen = [int(rng.integers(len(points)))]
    while len(chosen) < k:
        nearest = squared_distances(points, points[chosen]).min(axis=1)
        if nearest.max() == 0:  # every distinct location is already a center
            chosen.append(next(i for i in range(len(points)) if i not in chosen))
        else:
            chosen.append(int(rng.choice(len(points), p=nearest / nearest.sum())))
    return points[chosen].copy(), chosen

                validation_labels, fit_model(training[rows], k, 7).predict(validation)
            )
            for rows in bootstrap_rows
        ]
        minimum_size = int(np.bincount(fitted[1].labels_, minlength=k).min())
        median_stability = float(np.median(stability))
        validation_error = float(np.mean(fitted.transform(validation).min(axis=1) ** 2))
        eligible = minimum_size >= 20 and median_stability >= 0.8 and count > 1
        print(
            "candidate k / validation silhouette / mean squared distance / median ARI / min train size / eligible:",
            k,
            round(silhouette, 6),
            round(validation_error, 6),
            round(median_stability, 6),
            minimum_size,
            eligible,
        )
        if eligible:
            candidates.append((silhouette, -k, fitted, k))
    if not candidates:
        raise RuntimeError(
            "No candidate meets the predeclared requirements; revise the plan without using test results."
        )
    _, _, fitted, k = max(candidates, key=lambda row: row[:2])
    # Test data first enter here. No refit or changed k after reading this report.
    labels = fitted.predict(test)
    baseline = fit_model(training, 1, 7)
    error = float(np.mean(fitted.transform(test).min(axis=1) ** 2))
    baseline_error = float(np.mean(baseline.transform(test).min(axis=1) ** 2))
    centers = fitted[0].inverse_transform(fitted[1].cluster_centers_)
    print("selected k:", k)
    print(
        "test / training-centroid baseline mean squared standardized distance:",
        round(error, 6),
        round(baseline_error, 6),
    )
    print(
        "profiles ordered by fitted center temperature: count / mean temperature / mean vibration"
    )
    for cluster in np.argsort(centers[:, 0]):
        members = test[labels == cluster]
        if len(members):
            print(len(members), *np.round(members.mean(axis=0), 6).tolist())
        else:
            print(0, "no held-out members")
    # A transparent resource calculation, not a measured runtime prediction.
    future_n = 100000
    condensed_gib = (future_n * (future_n - 1) // 2) * 8 / 2**30
    print(
        "100000 rows: float64 condensed distance buffer alone (GiB):",
        round(condensed_gib, 3),
    )

        "A 16 GiB machine cannot hold that dense hierarchy plan; the reasoning belongs before fitting."

# K-Means & Hierarchical Clustering — lesson design and implementation

Scope authorized 11 September 2026: the next single topic, `k-means-hierarchical-clustering`, Classical Machine Learning position 11 of 39. Retain the title: metric choice, initialization, quantization and linkage are necessary parts of these two methods, not a reason to enumerate applications in the heading. Preserve its stable ID, memberships and position. The previous first-ten increment remains closed.

## Learning contract

A learner can calculate an assignment and mean update, distinguish a fitted partition from discovered truth, justify a distance representation, explain and implement careful seeding, read and cut a dendrogram with the correct height convention, choose an appropriate flat or hierarchical workflow, and submit a reproducible clustering report with limitations.

Prerequisite: the implemented K-Nearest Neighbors lesson supplies vectors, distance, units and training-owned transformations. This lesson refreshes squared distance and arithmetic means locally; it does not require a previous clustering course. NumPy code is explained with shapes. The beginner route reaches both complete algorithms and interpretable output; mathematical proofs and specialist connections are progressive branches, not substitutes for core reasoning.

Anchor: represent observations as points and choose a small set of representatives or a nested grouping. Preserve the original six labeled points P0=(1,0), P1=(1.5,.5), P2=(3,2), P3=(3.5,2), P4=(7,5), P5=(7.5,5.5). Preserve the original 150-observation `make_blobs` generator as a clearly synthetic library comparison. Use independently changed rectangles, axis scales and a constructed color raster to test transfer. No synthetic fixture establishes natural categories, clinical validity or a general implementation-speed ranking.

## Retain, repair and scope ownership

The entire old lesson was reviewed by the author and research reviewer. [Immutable original bytes](evidence/k-means-hierarchical-baseline.json) permit a coverage comparison; removing an incorrect statement is not removal of a curriculum topic.

| Existing idea / discovery | Decision and depth | Destination |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Objectives, Voronoi assignment, mean minimizer, Lloyd convergence | Retain and derive; repair strict-decrease and boundedness-only termination argument; declare ties, empty centers and early stopping | Core, sections 2–4 |
| k-means++ theory and scratch code | Retain complete runnable code; distinguish vanilla D² expectation guarantee from greedy sklearn seeding; handle duplicate/all-zero cases | Core seeding and deeper guarantee |
| All four linkage criteria, Ward scratch code and SciPy tree | Retain; distinguish ΔSSE, sqrt(2Δ) height, ordinary distance, exact merge-count cuts and tied-height cuts | Core hierarchical route |
| 150-point demo, trajectories, elbow, silhouette, distance matrix | Replace hand-authored numbers and a mislabeled 45-point plot with computed examples/figures. Diagnostics support a decision, not a certificate of true k | Core examples and validation bridge |
| Scaling, outliers, initialization, high-dimensional geometry, unequal groups, arbitrary labels | Retain with explicit mechanisms/counterexamples and reasonable boundaries; no always-scale rule or automatic anomaly label | Core diagnosis |
| Quantization and image palettes | Deepen: weighted repeated colors, centroid versus stored byte palette, actual distortion and honest bit accounting | This topic: direct objective application |
| ANN coarse codebooks, mini-batches and clustering features | Explain enough to map assignment to routing/stream summaries; show approximation limits and memory arithmetic | This topic with links for deeper systems work |
| BIRCH, medoids, spherical/kernel k-means, GMM and graph/density alternatives | Retain scoped mechanisms and selection boundaries; correct count-weight and covariance-limit claims | Deeper branches and actual existing follow-ons |
| PCA/UMAP as preprocessing and automatic biological interpretation | Replace blanket advice with representation/validation reasoning. PCA lesson is the actual next page; its own derivation remains there | Linked next topic; scoped destination note if a new useful instruction is needed |
| Silhouette, label permutations, stability and reference labels | Teach minimum needed to report results, with changed exercises. The existing evaluation topic explicitly owns full metric derivations, ARI/NMI and selection uncertainty | Destination note for clustering evaluation; do not rewrite it here |
| Long unsupported historical priority/popularity assertions | Keep sourced useful quantization/history connection; remove unsupported priority, universal performance and popularity claims | References / application explanation |

The scoped owner check inspected KNN's actual current blueprint and lesson, the PCA and GMM introductions and the clustering evaluation source. It is not an audit of every curriculum entry.

## Hurdles, representations and learning evidence

| Hurdle | Explanation / example | Representation and learner action | Independent evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No labels does not mean no assumptions | Representation, metric and k determine the question | Observation → feature vector → distance → partition, with center/group terminology | Diagnose a misleading customer segmentation |
| Two coupled unknowns | Freeze centers to assign, freeze assignments to take means | Lloyd phase map with point-center segments, old/new centers and exact current objective | Changed hand calculation and nonoptimal rectangle fixed point |
| Units define similarity | Squared axis differences receive squared scale factors | Feature-geometry comparison in the actual transformed coordinates | Convert a unit with and without the compensating weight |
| Random seeding is not farthest-first | D² defines probability mass, not a deterministic ranking | Cumulative sampling strip tied to actual points; zero-mass state explicit | Calculate probabilities and all-duplicate behavior |
| A hierarchy is a sequence of irreversible decisions | Different linkages ask different pair questions | Dendrogram and labeled scatter connected to selected merge prefix or height | Changed pair sets, tied-height cut and row-order interpretation |
| Ward has two commonly conflated quantities | Parallel-axis identity gives Δ; SciPy height is sqrt(2Δ) | Merge table/caption exposes both units next to tree | Direct union SSE versus Δ, and native SciPy comparison |
| Small error does not select the task | More centers can represent more detail | Actual native seed/k diagnostics, named metrics and failure examples | Explain local-fit nonmonotonicity, silhouette limits and stability |
| A representative has a concrete use | Replace each RGB vector by its palette entry | Original/reconstructed pixel mosaic with counts and calculated distortion | Weighted unique colors versus repeated pixels; storage caveats |
| A fitted model must be usable and evaluated | Fit transformations/centers on development data, freeze and report | Complete native pipeline and cluster profile output | Changed held-out capstone and explained diagnosis |

Each visual has a distinct purpose and runs bounded calculations on small fixtures. Geometry represents the displayed metric; dendrogram leaf spacing is layout, not distance. Numerical tables and member labels supplement color. Controls must be keyboard usable with reset/back behavior and legible narrow layouts. There is no lab quota. Static explanatory figures remain visible beside their concepts; optional details cannot conceal the first explanation.

## Implementation and evidence ownership

Six stages follow the [canonical workflow](../../LESSON-TEACHING-STANDARD.md#six-stage-authoring-workflow); quality-first guidance permits further relevant improvement at any stage.

- Author/integration owner: root. Lesson body, blueprint, scoped notes, metadata, browser review and final handoff.
- Research/coverage reviewer: scientific_visual_improvements. Complete original read; primary claims and annotated alternate resources in [source review](K-MEANS-HIERARCHICAL-SOURCE-REVIEW.md). Later independent complete-lesson review must be recorded separately from research.
- Native-example author: testing_documentation_completion. Complete Python programs and their executed outputs; independent native oracles/changed fixtures, with explicit runtime versions.
- Visual/model author: workflow_visual_improvements. Topic-native components, pure models and meaningful invariants; their own tests are author evidence, not independent review.

Current stage: complete, 11 September 2026. All six authoring stages are closed: assessment/research, complete implementation, author verification, independent review, focused corrections/browser closure, and website integration/handoff. The full production browser pass and subsequent focused label-layout amendment succeeded. No material finding remains open. User acceptance is separate; the next module topic is PCA and awaits the user's next scope.

Planned checks are source-bound rather than a campaign to rerun unchanged historical work: mean and Ward identities, exact small-fixture partition comparison, duplicate/tie/early-stop contracts, common unit-scale invariants, current native library output, browser controls and diagram interpretation at desktop/390px/keyboard, strict module sequence and ID/publication conservation, selected-topic lazy closure, production build. No benchmark claims will be inferred from schematic curves. Reading/practice estimates will be set after the complete material exists.

## Implemented learning experience

The fourteen-section route moves from choosing meaningful features through assignment/mean updates, metric choice, initialization, linkage and tree cuts to diagnosis, useful applications, changed practice and a complete held-out capstone. Mathematical proofs and specialist connections extend the visible beginner explanation. Retained depth includes the mean identity, careful seeding guarantee, empty/tied cases, Ward's two scales, all four linkages, current library workflows, mini-batches, weighted palettes, clustering features and approximate-search routing. The original six-point and 150-row examples remain identifiable.

Five investigations use different representations: assignment/residual geometry; transformed feature geometry; a D² sampling strip linked to points; an operable dendrogram with exact merge/count cuts; and a reconstructed color mosaic. Four inline figures explain the mean, linkage definitions, measured diagnostics and the ring counterexample. Nine changed exercises include hints and reasoned solutions. Six standalone Python programs expose their actual executed output, and the capstone includes an independent variation rather than asking the learner to copy the demonstrated result.

References contain annotated primary documentation, original research, educational articles and a direct MIT lecture/YouTube alternative. The [source review](K-MEANS-HIERARCHICAL-SOURCE-REVIEW.md) records the actual reviewed material, including the official lecture transcript; this is not a claim that the video was watched. Root additionally read the linked scikit-learn clustering-assumptions tutorial and dendrogram example. The lesson remains self-contained.

Newly useful follow-on instructions were saved for [PCA](topic-notes/pca-dimensionality-reduction.md) and [clustering evaluation](topic-notes/clustering-evaluation-validation-silhouette-ari-nmi.md). Future authors must assess their reasoning; neither destination was rewritten or automatically declared reviewed. PCA is the actual next module entry, regardless of publication state.

## Evidence and resolved findings

- [Native execution packet](evidence/k-means-hierarchical-native.json): six full programs, 49 changed oracle cases and five rejection cases, with NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.18.1 and scikit-learn 1.9.1. A later focused Ward repair retains the original execution identity and reruns only its affected program, five boundaries and three library fixtures.
- [Pure-model author packet](evidence/k-means-hierarchical-models.json): exact small-fixture objectives, linkage, seeding, weights, cuts and reconstruction checks, with focused arithmetic amendments and archived original evidence. The visible UI is a bounded teaching model, not a general arbitrary-range numerical library.
- [Complete independent lesson review](K-MEANS-HIERARCHICAL-INDEPENDENT-REVIEW.md): original/replacement coverage, all complete programs, prose, mathematics and visual source, plus complementary calculations. Findings about the first Python execution bridge and Ward underflow are closed. The first-time learner now receives environment/install/save/run guidance; unrepresentable positive squared costs produce a rescaling error instead of false coincidence.
- [Independent model and visual review](K-MEANS-HIERARCHICAL-VISUAL-MODEL-REVIEW.md): fourteen changed library/rational/weighted cases and comparison of every diagnostic row to actual native output. The stopped-seeding caption and arithmetic-range findings are closed. Its later opened-image finding is tracked separately from the already completed numerical review.
- [Full production browser pass before the label-only amendment](archive/k-means-hierarchical-before-label-layout/k-means-hierarchical-browser.json): twelve passing cases against Edge 152. All six displayed programs/outputs, fourteen anchors, controls and reset/back, keyboard ranges, narrow 390/320 layouts, exact module order, stable completion, selected-topic loading and import/render recovery were operated. A real label/input association defect was repaired before this pass: the range now has an explicit unique input ID and associated label/output.
- [Latest production evidence](evidence/k-means-hierarchical-browser.json) binds the current checked source/build and retained earlier evidence. The final build passed in 17.52 seconds, followed by 54 focused annotation states across 1366/390/320 widths. Root and the independent visual reviewer opened the corrected [desktop Lloyd](evidence/k-means-lloyd-desktop.png), [phone Lloyd](evidence/k-means-lloyd-mobile.png) and [seeding](evidence/k-means-seeding-desktop.png) captures. Point and center labels are readable, leaders identify unchanged markers, and the original collision finding is closed. Selected tree, mean, diagnostic and palette captures retain their earlier review. DOM overlap checks were supplemented by actual image interpretation.

Revisions were driven by those concrete findings. Source hashes identify what was checked; they do not replace reasoning or numerical/rendered evidence. Unchanged native, mathematical and reader checks are reused rather than relabeled as fresh executions after a CSS or annotation change.

## Integration boundaries and handoff

Curriculum and generated-artifact checks passed: 28 modules, 1,218 stable topic IDs, 352 individual briefs, seven guided paths, 228 publication mappings and 245 separately loaded outlines. Classical ML remains 39 topics and this lesson stays at position 11, after Survival Analysis and before PCA. Only this topic's selected body and actual shared dependencies load on its fresh reader route; no unrelated lesson body or syllabus outline was requested.

Production builds use the installed Vite entry directly because this machine's global npm shim is unavailable. Existing warnings in the untouched Bayesian Networks lesson and the shared navigation chunk remain outside this change. Browser payload figures are built file sizes and gzip estimates, not measured network compression, latency or a device-performance benchmark. Browser checks loaded the site's intended Google Fonts through the verification environment; no application network or security configuration was changed.

The final selected-route JavaScript total is 1,448,219 built bytes, with a 325,636-byte gzip estimate, including the actual shared runtime/navigation/math dependencies. The final label layout retains bounded fixed-fixture work and disconnects its resize observer on unmount. It does not alter the numerical model or displace plotted data to make labels fit.

The eight reviewed production sources are bound in [the completed scoped ledger](classical-ml-unsupervised-progress.json); the inventory reflects this exact-source implementation review. Retained captures, original source, compact evidence and small finding archives support future work without reopening completed suites. Three disposable working files were removed: the final build log, the failed temporary label-harness log and that superseded harness. Its honest failed outcome remains in the [layout amendment](evidence/k-means-label-layout-amendment.json); it is not counted as a successful check. The temporary production preview was stopped; the user's development preview and unrelated work were preserved.

There is no remaining implementation action in this increment. User acceptance remains separate, and no deployment was performed. The next request may authorize PCA, but this one-topic increment does not.

## Proposed revision, 12 September 2026 — awaiting the user's decision

The user asked for an independent quality opinion on the completed lesson and then for the resulting plan to be implemented so the result could be judged. The revision below is implemented in the working tree and is **not** committed, reviewed or accepted. The eight-source hashes in the earlier records and the ledger no longer describe the working tree; every displayed program was re-executed and the model, native and browser verifiers were rerun and pass on the new sources. Independent review of the changed prose, figures and labs has not happened.

Content changes: one caution callout in section 1 replaces the per-paragraph qualifications (disclaimer phrases roughly halved, from 27 to 19 across a longer body); an explicit first-pass route; the real Old Faithful dataset (272 rows, Härdle 1991 version via the R datasets mirror) introduced in section 1, fitted in section 8 and used for the k = 1..8 diagnostics on a logarithmic inertia axis; a forty-leaf SciPy Ward dendrogram of a deterministic subsample; the Lloyd/Ward 7.6875 coincidence made explicit with the Ward-initialized k-means trick; verified facts added with sources (NP-hardness of the objective, Vattani's exponential lower bound, smoothed polynomial iterations, Murtagh and Legendre on the two Ward conventions, centroid-linkage inversions, Lloyd's 1957 note); a changed-unit geyser exercise; a changed-seed capstone self-check drawn from the native oracle; ESL and ISLR added to the alternate resources. The displayed Python programs drop the arithmetic-underflow guards and printed moral sentences so the mechanisms stay visible; validation is a finiteness check, stated as such in prose.

Lab changes: every investigation records a prediction and compares it with the model's answer. Lloyd accepts any two seed rows, draws the nearest-center bisector and has a run-to-fixed-point control. Feature geometry enumerates all seven two-group splits instead of comparing two initializations. Seeding accepts successive D² draws and shows exact probability against 200 seeded draws and the uniform baseline. Hierarchy adds a chain-plus-triple fixture with exact unit spacing on which single and complete linkage disagree, plus merge stepping. Palette adds a 37-color sky raster and a 160-color gradient. New evidence captures are in `evidence/`; the old Lloyd, seeding, tree, mean, diagnostics and palette captures were regenerated by the updated browser verifier.

If the user accepts, the next actions are: independent review against the new source identity, a refreshed source-bound ledger, and a commit. If the user declines, `git checkout -- .` and removal of the four untracked files restore the reviewed state.
